metadata.title: Visual Rhetoric Database
metadata.description: Comprehensive reference database for visual rhetorical analysis and construction

schema.overview: This division governs the systematic five-stage workflow used to transform a visual concept into a fully realized and rendered piece of media (poster, film, or digital content).
schema.core_question: How do I turn an idea for a visual text into a finished artefact?

inventio.name: Invention/Discovery
inventio.definition: The discovery and brainstorming phase where you identify the strongest visual motifs, subject matter, and data points available for your project.
key_characteristics: Research of visual references and inspiration
Discovery of relevant imagery and symbols
Analysis of visual data and source material
examples: A filmmaker collecting reference images and creating a mood board before production
A graphic designer researching visual trends and competitor designs
A photographer scouting locations and planning shot lists

dispositio.name: Arrangement
dispositio.definition: The strategic arrangement of visual elements into a coherent layout or sequence (such as shot composition, hierarchy, and editing) to maximize impact.
examples: A poster designed with clear visual hierarchy from headline to call-to-action
A film edited with strategic shot sequencing to build tension
A website layout using grid systems and visual flow

elocutio.name: Style
elocutio.definition: The stylistic 'texture' of the visual, focusing on aesthetic choices like color grading, typography, lighting, and art direction to suit the target audience.
examples: Film noir using high-contrast black and white cinematography
A brand identity using specific color schemes and typefaces
Instagram filters creating a consistent aesthetic across images

memoria.name: Memory
memoria.definition: The use of visual motifs, brand guidelines, and thematic consistency to ensure the message remains recognizable and conceptually coherent across the entire work.
examples: A film series using consistent color motifs (e.g., blue in The Matrix)
Corporate branding maintaining logo and color consistency
A director's signature visual style across multiple films

pronuntiatio.name: Delivery/Performance
pronuntiatio.definition: The final execution and exhibition of the media, focusing on technical resolution, audio-visual sync, performance, and the physical or digital delivery to the viewer.
examples: A film released in IMAX format for maximum visual impact
A digital advertisement optimized for mobile viewing
A gallery exhibition with careful lighting and placement

proofs.overview: These represent the primary modes of persuasion used to establish visual validity and influence the perspective or behavior of the viewer.
proofs.core_question: What specific types of visual evidence and aesthetic appeals must I employ to establish my authority and convince the viewer that my message is true?

ethos.name: Visual Credibility
ethos.definition: Establishing credibility and trust by using professional aesthetics, authoritative symbols (logos, uniforms), and high-production value to demonstrate expertise and reliability.
examples: A corporate video using high-end production and professional talent
A doctor wearing a white coat and stethoscope in medical advertising
News graphics using official logos and professional design

pathos.name: Visual Emotion
pathos.definition: Generating credibility and engagement by appealing to the viewer's emotions through visceral imagery, music, and color palettes that create an empathetic connection.
examples: Charity campaigns showing images of suffering to evoke compassion
Sunset imagery in romantic films creating warmth and nostalgia
Dark, desaturated colors in horror films evoking fear

logos.name: Visual Logic
logos.definition: Building credibility through clear data visualization, infographics, and sequential logical flow in editing to support a rational, evidence-based conclusion.
examples: An infographic showing statistical trends with clear graphs
A tutorial video showing step-by-step processes
Before-and-after images demonstrating product effectiveness

tropes.overview: This division involves the creative 'turning' of imagery—using visual elements in non-literal ways to shift meaning and engage the viewer's imagination.
tropes.core_question: How can I transform standard imagery into imaginative visual figures to make a concept feel richer, more evocative, and conceptually deep?

resemblance.name: Visual Metaphor
resemblance.definition: Visual metaphors or similes where two distinct images are juxtaposed or blended to create meaning based on shared traits (e.g., a melting clock).
examples: Salvador Dalí's melting clocks (time as fluid/unstable)
A person's head replaced with a lightbulb (representing ideas)
Hands forming a dove shape (peace through unity)

association.name: Visual Metonymy
association.definition: Visual metonymy that uses a related object to represent a larger concept (e.g., showing a gavel to represent the entire judicial system).
examples: A gavel representing justice/law
A crown representing monarchy/royalty
The Eiffel Tower representing Paris/France

naming.name: Visual Synecdoche
naming.definition: Visual synecdoche where a part of an object identifies the whole, such as showing only the wheels of a car to represent a journey.
examples: Showing only feet walking to represent a journey
Close-up of hands shaking to represent agreement
Just the wheels of a car to represent transportation

invention.name: Visual Innovation
invention.definition: The creative stretching of visual 'grammar,' such as glitch art, surreal distortions, or using color in non-naturalistic ways to describe the 'indescribable.'
examples: Glitch art using digital artifacts creatively
Abstract expressionism in visual design
Impossible architecture in M.C. Escher's work

extendedmeaning.name: Visual Allegory
extendedmeaning.definition: Large-scale visual figures like allegory or visual irony where the surface imagery masks a deeper, sustained secondary narrative.
examples: Hieronymus Bosch paintings with moral allegories
Political cartoons with layered symbolism
Music videos with sustained metaphorical narratives

ornamentalepithet.name: Visual Tags
ornamentalepithet.definition: The use of signature visual 'tags' or recurring stylistic flourishes that characterize a person or object with vivid, recognizable intensity.
examples: Wes Anderson's symmetrical framing and pastel palettes
Michael Bay's 'bayhem' explosion aesthetics
Banksy's stencil art style

fallacies.overview: This division focuses on the coherence of the meaning or message being communicated.
fallacies.core_question: What sort of argument is being presented or failing to be presented?

fallacy.name: Visual Logical Errors
fallacy.definition: Identifying and labeling common errors in visual reasoning—such as misleading edits, out-of-context imagery, or deceptive 'Photoshopping'—that derail logical truth.

common_types.name: False Context
common_types.description: Using images out of their original context to mislead
common_types.example: A cropped photo removing context that changes the meaning

common_types.name: Selective Framing
common_types.example: Cropping out empty seats at a rally to suggest larger attendance

common_types.name: Misleading Edit
common_types.description: Sequential editing that creates false causation
common_types.example: News footage edited to suggest false chronology or causation

common_types.name: Manipulated Imagery
common_types.example: Celebrity photos heavily retouched to set unrealistic standards

common_types.name: False Scale
common_types.example: Graphs with manipulated scales to exaggerate trends

common_types.name: Cherry-picked Visuals
common_types.example: Before/after images using different lighting to exaggerate results

common_types.name: Staged Authenticity
common_types.example: Reality TV presented as unscripted when it's heavily produced

common_types.name: Visual Straw Man
common_types.example: Using unflattering freeze-frames of political opponents

common_types.name: Emotional Manipulation
common_types.description: Using visceral imagery to bypass logic
common_types.example: Shocking images that provoke reaction without context

common_types.name: False Equivalence
common_types.example: Side-by-side images suggesting equal severity of unequal events

fallacy_flipside.name: Legitimate Visual Techniques
fallacy_flipside.definition: Recognizing legitimate uses of visual simplification or understanding the strategic ways to counter 'fake' imagery and return the work to rational ground.
examples: Artistic Compositing: Clearly artistic photo manipulations (album covers, art)
Accepted Enhancements: Standard color correction and exposure adjustment
Symbolic Simplification: Icons and diagrams that simplify for clarity
Dramatization Labels: Clearly labeled reenactments or dramatizations
Educational Visualization: Simplified models for teaching (not deception)
Creative Framing: Compositional choices for aesthetic (not deceptive) purposes
